newsitem.title: UK: London Transport yr operating surplus moves ahead.
newsitem.headline: London Transport yr operating surplus moves ahead.

text.p: London Transport, the public sector operator behind the capital's metro and bus network, reported continued progress in its annual results on Thursday, with the operating surplus up 39 million stg on the previous year.
The year operating surplus for the 1996/97 financial year was 169 million stg despite the London Underground metro system suffering strike action during the period.

Peter Ford, London Transport chairman, welcomed the figures and said this was the fifth consecutive year of progress which had taken the network from a 130 million stg deficit five years ago to a 169 million surplus.
During the last financial year 1.06 billion stg was invested in the network of which 660 million went into the Jubilee Line extension.
The total government grant was 921 million, but London Transport said that for the third year in a row it did not require a subsidy for its day-to-day operations.

Speaking at the results press conference, Ford used the opportunity to repeat the need for a speedy solution to the funding crisis impacting on the metro system. The government is currently reviewing a number of options including full-blown privatisation of London Underground.

He said London Transport chiefs were in urgent talks with the new Labour government ministers to solve the problem which was exacerbated by a cut in funding introduced in the last Conservative government budget in November.
"We will be working with the government to investigate the best solutions over the next few weeks," he said.
"I think it is clear the deputy prime minister (John Prescott) and the transport minister (Gavin Strang) are aware of the problem and consider it a high priority," he said.
But he added that it was too soon to say which possible solution was the front-runner in discussions.

Asked whether failure to solve the metro's funding crisis would lead to major upsets like line-closures, Denis Tunnicliffe, managing director of London Underground, said "There are no doomsday scenarios -- we are skilled at managing a deteriorating asset. But without new money we will continue to see problems, breakdowns."
